verdicts.why: Physical elevation ('high woody hills') is a measurement, not an attitude toward what is measured.
'High spirits' names a mood; any judgement in the packet sentence comes from 'oppressively', not from 'high'.
Greater-than-normal amount ('high price', 'high opinion') is a scale reading; the word takes no side about the thing scaled.
Pitch is an acoustic fact; 'high voice' neither approves nor dismisses the speaker.
'High' is the plain everyday word for drug or drink intoxication, informal in register but carrying no contempt or approval beyond the state it names.
A bad referent (tainted meat) in a plain word; 'high' is the standard term for hung game and does not add disgust the way 'putrid' would.
Names an unpleasant state ('anxious attention', 'anxious curiosity') without judging the person in it; the referent is bad, the word is not loaded.
This is the ordinary/usual sense ('common cold', 'not out of the common way'); the contemptuous 'vulgar, low-class' senses of common are separate synsets not printed here.
Shared between parties ('in common with others') is a relation, not an appraisal.
Frequency ('a very common failing') states how often something occurs and nothing about how the speaker feels toward it.
Belonging to the community as a whole ('common good', 'common land') is a plain civic description.
To be expected; standard ('common decency', 'common courtesy') describes a norm without contempt or praise for what meets it.
Of everyday language ('common parlance') is a neutral register label; the loaded synonym in this synset would be 'vulgar', not 'common'.
Membership of the hereditary aristocracy ('noble birth', 'noble kindred') is a statement of rank; Austen applies it flatly even to Lady Catherine, whom she is mocking.
A chemistry term (noble gases, noble metals) with no attitude toward the element.
Free from stress ('not comfortable on this subject') describes a pleasant state plainly; the good referent is the meaning, not a layer of approval on top of it.
'A comfortable income' says the amount is sufficient for ease; that adequacy is the definition itself, not an attitude beyond it.
A wide margin ('a comfortable lead') is a description of size; the word does not favour the leader.
Volume ('speak lower', 'a low voice') is a physical quality with no judgement of the speaker.
Small elevation ('a low phaeton', 'its lowest points') is measurement; the socially contemptuous 'low connections' belongs to a different synset not printed here.
Less than normal in amount ('low price', 'low temperature') is a scale reading, not an appraisal.
Pitch is an acoustic fact; 'low voice' takes no side.
'Supplies are low' reports a shortfall in plain words; the referent may be unwelcome but the word carries no attitude.
'Worthy of being chosen' is an evaluation by definition, shared with its synonyms 'suitable' and 'worthy'; the approval is the gloss itself, not a warning the learner needs beyond it.
Having a specified value ('worth ten pounds', 'not worth hearing') states an equivalence; any judgement lives in what follows the word, not in it.
A fixed letter-closing formula, conventional and attitude-free in the sense printed.
Fight verbally in a light, sporting way ('the candidates sparred over taxes'); the lightness is the meaning inherited from boxing practice, not contempt or approval of the parties.
Box lightly is a plain sporting term.
Fight with spurs (of gamecocks) is a plain description of the action.
Furnish a vessel with spars is a technical rigging term with no attitude.
